question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=-6{e}^{-2t}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m/s}$)  of the particle at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-6{e}^{-2t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t})+C \\  & =3{e}^{-2t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =3{e}^{0}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{e}^{-2t}-1.$

evidence.solution_quote: Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{e}^{-2t}-1.$
